sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage C
sections.intro: Read “Sweet, Sour, and Resentful” and answer questions 15–24. Vocabulary notes follow the passage.

passage.title: Sweet, Sour, and Resentful
passage.credit: —Firoozeh Dumas · “Sweet, Sour, and Resentful” · Gourmet Magazine, July 2009

lines.text: My mother’s main ingredient in cooking was resentment—not that I can blame her.
In 1979, my family was living temporarily in Newport Beach, California. Our real home
was in Abadan, a city in the southwest of Iran. Despite its desert location and ubiquitous¹
refineries, Abadan was the quintessential² small town. Everybody’s father (including my
own) worked for the National Iranian Oil Company, and almost all the moms stayed home.
The employees’ kids attended the same schools. No one locked their doors. Whenever
I hear John Mellencamp’s “Small Town,” I think of Abadan, although I’m guessing John
Mellencamp was thinking of somewhere else when he wrote that song.
By the time of the Iranian revolution,³ we had adjusted to life in California. We said
“Hello” and “Have a nice day” to perfect strangers, wore flip-flops, and grilled cheeseburgers
next to our kebabs. We never understood why Americans put ice in tea or bought shampoo
that smelled like strawberries, but other than that, America felt like home.
When the revolution happened, thousands left Iran for Southern California. Since we
were one of the few Iranian families already there, our phone did not stop ringing. Relatives,
friends, friends of relatives, friends of friends, and people whose connection we never
quite figured out called us with questions about settling into this new land. Displaying the
hospitality that Iranians so cherish, my father extended a dinner invitation to everyone who
called. As a result, we found ourselves feeding dozens of people every weekend.
The marathon started on Monday, with my mother planning the menu while letting us
know that she was already tired. Fortunately, our rice dishes were made to be shared; our
dilemma, however, was space. Our condo was small. Our guests squeezed onto the sofa, sat
on the floor, or overflowed onto the patio. We eventually had to explain to our American
neighbors why there were so many cars parked in front of our place every weekend. My
mother, her diplomatic skills in full swing, had me deliver plates of Persian food, decorated
with radish roses and mint sprigs, to them. In time, we learned not to share fesenjan,
pomegranate stew with ground walnuts. “Yes, now that you mention it, it does look like mud,
but it’s really good,” I’d explain, convincing no one.
Because my mother did not drive, my father took her to buy ingredients every Tuesday
after work. In Abadan, my mother and I had started most days in the market, going from
vendor to vendor looking for herbs, vegetables, and fruits. The fish came from the Karun and
Arvand (Shatt al Arab) rivers, the lavash and the sangak breads were freshly baked, and the
chickens were still alive. We were locavores⁴ by necessity and foodies without knowing it. In
America, I learned that the time my parents spent shopping was in direct correlation to the
degree of my mother’s bad mood. An extra-long trip meant that my mother could not find
everything she needed, a point she would make loud and clear when she got home: “Why
don’t they let fruit ripen here?” “Why are the chickens so huge and flavorless?” “I couldn’t
find fresh herbs.” “My feet hurt.” “How am I supposed to get everything done?”
The first step was preparing the herbs. My mother insisted that the parsley, cilantro, and
chives for qormeh sabzi, herb stew, had to be finely chopped by hand. The food processor,
she explained, squished them. As she and my father sat across the table wielding huge knives,
they argued incessantly. My father did his best to help her. It wasn’t enough. As soon as
the mountain of herbs was chopped, my mother started frying them. At any given time, my
mother was also frying onions. Every few days, while my father was watching the six o’clock
news, my mother would hand him a dozen onions, a cutting board, and a knife. No words
were exchanged. Much to my father’s relief, I once volunteered for this task, but apparently
my slices were neither thin enough nor even. It took my father’s precision as an engineer to
slice correctly.
While all four burners were in use, my mother mixed the ground beef, rice, split peas,
scallions, and herbs for stuffed grape leaves. I chopped the stems of the grape leaves. I had
tried stuffing them once, but my rolls, deemed not tight enough, were promptly unrolled
and then rerolled by my mother.
In between cooking, my mother made yogurt—the thick, sour variety that we couldn’t
find in America. She soaked walnuts and almonds in water to plump them up; fried eggplants
for kashk-e bademjan, a popular appetizer with garlic, turmeric, mint, and whey; made
torshi-e limo, a sour lemon condiment; and slivered orange peels. I had been fired from this
task also, having left on far too much pith.⁵
By the time our guests arrived, my mother was exhausted. But the work was not finished.
Rice, the foundation of the Persian meal, the litmus test⁶ of the cook’s ability, cannot be
prepared ahead of time. To wit,⁷ one day in Abadan, the phone rang when my mother was
about to drain the rice. During the time it took her to answer the phone and tell her sister
that she would call her back, the rice overcooked. Almost 40 years later, I still remember
my mother’s disappointment and her explaining to my father that her sister had time to talk
because my aunt’s maid did all the cooking. My aunt did not even drain her own rice.
We certainly did not have a table big enough to set, so we simply stacked dishes and
utensils, buffet-style. As the guest list grew, we added paper plates and plastic utensils. It
was always my job to announce that dinner was ready. As people entered the dining room,
they gasped at the sight of my mother’s table. Her zereshk polow, barberry rice, made many
emotional. There are no fresh barberries in America (my mother had brought dried berries
from Iran in her suitcase), and the sight of that dish, with its distinct deep red hue, was a
reminder of the life our guests had left behind.
Our dinners took days to cook and disappeared in 20 minutes. As our guests heaped their
plates and looked for a place to sit, they lavished praise on my mother, who, according to
tradition, deflected it all. “It’s nothing,” she said. “I wish I could’ve done more.” When they
told her how lucky she was to have me to help her, my mother politely nodded, while my
father added, “Firoozeh’s good at math.”
On Sundays, my mother lay on the sofa, her swollen feet elevated, fielding thank-you
phone calls from our guests. She had the same conversation a dozen times; each one ended
with, “Of course you can give our name to your cousins.” As I watched my mother experience
the same draining routine week after week, I decided that tradition is good only if it brings
joy to all involved. This includes the hostess. Sometimes, even our most cherished beliefs
must evolve. Evolution, thy name is potluck.⁸
¹ ubiquitous — abundant
² quintessential — typical
³ Iranian revolution — in 1979, the Iranian monarchy was replaced by a religious dictatorship
⁴ locavores — people whose diet consists of locally grown food
⁵ pith — the spongy, bitter portion of a citrus fruit rind
⁶ litmus test — absolute indication
⁷ to wit — for example
⁸ potluck — a meal to which each of the guests contributes a dish

questions.prompt: Which quotation supports the statement “My mother’s main ingredient in cooking was resentment—not that I can blame her” (line 1)?

choices.text: “Our real home was in Abadan, a city in the southwest of Iran” (lines 2 and 3)
“We never understood why Americans put ice in tea or bought shampoo that smelled like strawberries” (lines 11 and 12)
“When the revolution happened, thousands left Iran for Southern California” (line 13)
“Displaying the hospitality that Iranians so cherish, my father extended a dinner invitation to everyone who called” (lines 16 through 18)

questions.explanation: The father invites every caller to dinner, creating a weekly obligation for his wife to feed dozens of people. That detail directly explains why she resents the cooking burden while the narrator sympathizes with her.

questions.prompt: According to lines 3 through 8, life in the city of Abadan could best be described as

choices.text: challenging
traditional
exciting
unpredictable

questions.explanation: The narrator remembers a familiar small-town pattern: fathers worked for the oil company, mothers generally stayed home, children attended the same schools, and neighbors left doors unlocked. This stable, conventional routine is best described as traditional.

questions.prompt: The details in lines 9 through 12 emphasize the family’s

choices.text: suspicion of their American neighbors
distress after the upheaval
desire to return to their homeland
adaptation to the American way of life

questions.explanation: The family greets strangers, wears flip-flops, and grills cheeseburgers along with kebabs. Despite a few customs they find strange, America has begun to feel like home, showing adaptation.

choices.text: desire to maintain the values of his culture
need to become successful in his new country
discomfort with adjusting to American customs
reluctance with assisting other immigrants

questions.explanation: The narrator explicitly links the father's invitations to hospitality that Iranians cherish. Offering meals to new arrivals preserves that cultural value, even though the workload falls on the family.

questions.prompt: The use of the word “marathon” (line 19) implies that the mother’s preparations are

choices.text: long and exhausting
expert and admirable
tedious but rewarding
unpleasant but necessary

questions.explanation: A marathon lasts a long time and demands stamina. The mother starts planning Monday for weekend dinners, says she is already tired, and remains exhausted when guests arrive.

questions.prompt: The rhetorical questions in lines 34 through 37 convey the mother’s

choices.text: irrational emotion
lack of confidence
increasing frustration
unwillingness to continue

questions.explanation: Unable to find familiar ingredients, the mother asks why fruit is unripe and chickens are flavorless, then worries about finishing everything. The accumulating complaints convey increasing frustration.

questions.prompt: The description in lines 45 through 47 highlights the

choices.text: father’s lack of connection to his wife
father’s assistance with meal preparation
mother’s stress about completing her task
mother’s independence when cooking

questions.explanation: The father cuts onions with the precision his wife requires; even the narrator's volunteered slices do not meet that standard. The detail shows his practical help in preparing meals.

questions.prompt: The narrator’s efforts to help the mother (lines 45 through 51) best demonstrate her

choices.text: interest in following her mother’s example
resentment toward her mother’s expertise
inability to meet her mother’s expectations
confidence about creating her mother’s dishes

questions.explanation: The narrator volunteers to slice onions, but the slices are not thin or even enough; her grape leaves are also unrolled and redone. These repeated rejections show she cannot meet her mother's exacting standards.

questions.prompt: The flashback presented in lines 59 through 63 reinforces the

choices.text: significance of rice in Persian cuisine
closeness of family relationships
sister’s superior cooking ability
mother’s sympathy for her sister’s life

questions.explanation: The mother still remembers a single batch of rice ruined by a brief phone call nearly forty years earlier. That enduring disappointment illustrates how important properly prepared rice is in the Persian meal.

questions.prompt: The guests’ reaction to seeing the barberry rice (lines 67 through 70) displays their

choices.text: nostalgia for the food of their country
surprise at the arrangement of the dishes
expression of respect to the host
recognition of the cost of the berries

questions.explanation: The red barberry rice makes many newly arrived guests emotional because its sight reminds them of life left behind in Iran. Their response is nostalgia for their homeland's food and memories.
